title: When the preview says zero and the data is there
subtitle: Redesigning a collaborative analytics platform for data analysts at top US, Canadian, and UK banks and insurers, inside a regulated financial-services environment

sections.headline: When the preview says zero and the data is there
sections.subtext: Five years designing a collaborative analytics platform for data analysts at top US, Canadian and UK banks and insurers, and moving design from executing specs to shaping what got built.

sections.headline: The starting point
sections.content:
When I joined Datameer in 2016, the platform's users were data analysts at top US, Canadian and UK banks and insurers: people who understood data deeply and needed the interface to get out of the way, not add cognitive load on top of already complex analytical work.

Design existed, but as an execution function. Designers received specs and turned them into screens, and user research was not yet part of how product decisions got made.

sections.quote: The preview showed empty results. The full data was there.
sections.context: The sample-based uncertainty problem: the hardest UX challenge on the platform

sections.headline: The core challenge
sections.content:
Big data analytics platforms have a built-in UX problem: when a dataset is too large to process in real time, the preview runs on a sample. And a sample can come back empty, not because the data isn't there, but because the sample didn't catch it.

Users would build a query, see empty results in the preview, and reasonably conclude their data was missing. The data was fine. The preview was misleading them, not through a bug, but through a property of sampled data.

That made it an information design problem, not a visual one: how do you represent uncertainty honestly without making people lose confidence in a tool they depend on every day?

images.alt: Diagram: a query against the full dataset returns real matches, but a preview built from a small sample can miss all of them and report zero — not a bug, a property of sampling itself.
images.caption: Why a sampled preview can report nothing while the data is sitting there.

steps.label: Customer Research
steps.description: With executive support for user research, I joined the sales team on a customer research trip and ran sessions in person with US banking and insurance customers. Where access was harder, iterative screening on usertesting.com found the hard-to-reach personas.

steps.label: Platform Redesign
steps.description: A complete UX and UI redesign of the analytics interface, from information architecture down to the details: column charts, big-data pivot tables, aggregated JSON views, result cards and a comprehensive filter system.

steps.label: Design System
steps.description: Co-built the platform's design system. I owned component behavior and interaction specs across the library, including details like data-table column headers, inspector panels and custom motion easing.

steps.label: Organizational Elevation
steps.description: Datameer was betting on a new product, and that bet needed research and design in the room where it was decided. Research got executive support, and design moved into the roadmap conversations.

sections.headline: Results

metrics.label: UX Maturity
metrics.after: Strategic partner, with executive support for user research

metrics.label: Design System
metrics.value: Co-built, with component behavior and interaction specs owned by UX

metrics.label: User Research
metrics.value: In-person sessions with US banking and insurance customers, plus remote screening for hard-to-reach personas

metrics.label: Sample Uncertainty UX
metrics.value: Visual and text feedback that tells users when a preview is a sample and how it differs from the full query

sections.narrative: The biggest change was organizational. Datameer kept its existing product and went after a new one, and that new product needed research and design where its direction was set. Research got executive backing, design entered the roadmap conversations, and the design system got built.

sections.headline: What I learned
sections.content:
The hardest part wasn't the design. Regulated banks and insurers limit who can watch their analysts work, so research needed executive backing and methods that worked around those limits before it could happen at all.

This experience shaped my conviction that you can't build good products without building the organization that supports them. Human-centered organizations make better products, because they actually talk to humans.

sections.headline: Why this matters for your team
sections.content: If you're building data-dense tools for technically sophisticated users in regulated environments, the design challenges are fundamentally different from consumer products. I've spent five years learning those differences, from sample-uncertainty communication to compliance-aware user research. This is transferable to any domain where the data is complex, the users are expert, and the stakes are high.

Ask me how a preview that reported zero results while the data sat right there turned out to be an information design problem, and how research with bank and insurance analysts got executive backing in the first place. Get in touch.

executive.summary: Took design from an execution function to a strategic partner at a big data analytics platform serving top US, Canadian and UK banks and insurers. Co-built the design system, owned component behavior and interaction specs, and solved the sample-uncertainty problem in query previews.
